Description: Define HOW your product is different and WHO it's for. Not tagline — strategic decision that shapes everything: messaging, pricing, features, sales.
Framework: April Dunford 5-Step: 1) Competitive Alternatives 2) Unique Attributes 3) Value (what attributes enable) 4) Best-Fit Customer 5) Market Category
Do_This: Start from competitive alternatives (what would customers do without you?)|Identify attributes ONLY you have|Map to value customers care about|Pick the category that makes your strengths obvious
Avoid_This: Starting with category (I'm a CRM)|Positioning by features not value|Trying to be everything to everyone|Copying competitor positioning
Example: Superhuman: not 'email client' but 'fastest email experience' — repositioned in 'speed' category instead of 'email' category

Description: Create a new category instead of competing in existing one. Category kings capture 76% of market value. High risk high reward.
Framework: Play Bigger Framework: 1) Define the problem your category solves 2) Name the category 3) Evangelize through content/events 4) Be first to own the category POV
Do_This: Only if genuinely new approach to a problem|Name the category simply|Educate market through content|Be prepared for 2-3 year investment
Avoid_This: Creating category for positioning sake (if existing category works, use it)|Confusing naming|Under-investing in category education
Example: Drift created 'Conversational Marketing' — didn't compete in 'live chat' category

Description: Map customer jobs, pains, gains → match with your product's pain relievers, gain creators, features. Visual tool for achieving product-market fit.
Framework: Value Proposition Canvas: Left = Customer Profile (jobs, pains, gains) | Right = Value Map (products, pain relievers, gain creators) | Goal = Fit
Do_This: Start with customer profile (not your product)|Validate each pain/gain with real data|Rank by importance to customer|Map your product only to top-priority items
Avoid_This: Starting with features (product-out thinking)|Listing all possible pains (focus on top 3)|No validation with real customers
Example: Strategyzer/Osterwalder — companion to Business Model Canvas

Description: Systematic hierarchy of messages: Positioning → Key Messages (3 max) → Proof Points → Headlines. Ensures consistency across all touchpoints.
Framework: Message Hierarchy: 1) One-liner positioning 2) 3 key messages (benefits) 3) Proof points per message (data, testimonials, cases) 4) Channel-specific headlines
Do_This: Write for the customer not for you|Test headlines with real users|Use customer language (from interviews)|3 messages maximum — more = diluted
Avoid_This: Feature-speak instead of benefit-speak|Different messaging per channel (inconsistency)|No proof points (claims without evidence)
Example: Linear: 'Built for the way software teams work' — one clear message, proven by speed + keyboard shortcuts + GitHub integration

Description: Define your best-fit customer with precision. Not demographics — behavior + problem + ability and willingness to pay. Narrow beats broad.
Framework: ICP Template: Industry + Company Size + Role + Problem + Current Solution + Budget + Decision Process + What Success Looks Like
Do_This: Start narrow (1 specific ICP)|Define by problem not demographics|Validate: would losing this product make them very disappointed?|Expand ICP only after dominating first niche
Avoid_This: Too broad ('all small businesses')|Demographics without behavior|Multiple ICPs before PMF|Not talking to actual ICP members
Example: Notion initially: small startups using wikis (not 'all companies') — expanded after PMF

Description: Plot competitors on 2 axes that matter to YOUR customer. Choose axes where you WIN. This is your strategic positioning weapon.
Framework: 2x2 Matrix: Choose 2 dimensions customers care about | Plot all competitors | Your position should be in the best quadrant | If not — change axes or change product
Do_This: Choose axes where you're differentiated|Use customer-validated dimensions (not internal)|Update quarterly|Share with team for alignment
Avoid_This: Using generic axes (price vs quality)|Axes where you lose|Not validating axes with customers|Static (never updating)
Example: Basecamp: 'Simple vs Complex' × 'All-in-one vs Fragmented' — wins in Simple + All-in-one quadrant

Description: Show the transformation: Before (pain state) → After (desired state). Your product is the bridge. Most effective messaging pattern.
Framework: Before/After/Bridge: 1) BEFORE — describe customer's painful reality 2) AFTER — describe desired state 3) BRIDGE — your product gets them there
Do_This: Use customer's own words for Before state|Make After state specific and measurable|Product is the bridge not the hero (customer is hero)
Avoid_This: Feature lists instead of transformation|Vague After state|Making product the hero (not the customer)
Example: Slack: Before = 'drowning in email' → After = 'organized team communication' → Bridge = Slack

Description: Define what you're NOT as clearly as what you ARE. Opinionated products attract loyal customers by repelling the wrong ones.
Framework: Anti-Positioning: 'We are X, NOT Y' | 'We believe [stance], unlike [conventional wisdom]' | 'We don't do [common feature] because [reason]'
Do_This: Take a clear stance|Be genuinely different (not just contrarian)|Back up anti-positions with philosophy|Accept you'll lose some customers
Avoid_This: Being contrarian without substance|Attacking competitors directly|Wishy-washy (trying to be both)|Changing stance too frequently
Example: Basecamp: 'We don't do Gantt charts because they create false precision' — opinionated, attracts right customers

Keywords: counter-positioning,structural anchor,revenue lock-in,process inertia,competitive moat,hamilton helmer,7 powers,incumbent disadvantage
Description: Identify what structurally prevents incumbents from copying you. Focus on 3 anchors: Revenue model lock-in (their subscription model prevents offering yours). Process inertia (their enterprise sales team cannot do self-serve). Conflict of interest (copying you would cannibalize their core business).
Framework: Hamilton Helmer 7 Powers — Counter-Positioning: new entrant adopts a superior business model that incumbent cannot copy because it would damage their existing business
Do_This: Map incumbent revenue model and ask: if they copied us would they lose existing revenue?|Identify process anchors: are they too large/slow/enterprise to serve our niche?|Find conflict of interest: does solving this problem hurt their other products?|Test: if Google built this tomorrow would they have to change something that hurts them?
Avoid_This: Competing on features alone (they have more engineers)|Assuming incumbents cannot copy (they can if no structural barrier)|Confusing brand positioning with counter-positioning (brand is perception structural is reality)
Example: Basecamp vs Salesforce: Basecamp flat /mo — Salesforce per-seat model cannot offer this without destroying their revenue. Structural anchor = per-seat billing lock-in.

Keywords: revenue verification,proxy data,willingness to pay,alternative spend,budget displacement,do nothing cost,market validation,revenue proxy
Description: Money is the most honest validation signal. If customers dont pay for any alternative solution (even bad ones) they likely wont pay for yours. Verify through: direct data (competitor revenue from annual reports) and proxy data (ad spend on related keywords staff salaries for manual workaround SaaS stack costs they combine as substitute).
Framework: IdeaValidator Revenue Proxy Method: 1) Check competitor revenue (Owler/Crunchbase) 2) Check ad spend (SimilarWeb) 3) Check salary of manual alternative (what staff do they hire to solve this?) 4) Check SaaS stack cost (what tools do they combine?)
Do_This: Use Owler/Crunchbase for competitor revenue estimates|Check SimilarWeb for traffic→revenue estimates (traffic × conversion × ARPU)|Look at job postings: if companies hire people to solve this problem manually the budget exists|Calculate combined SaaS stack cost customers pay for workaround tools
Avoid_This: Assuming market exists without revenue evidence|Using only TAM top-down estimates|Ignoring that free alternatives mean low willingness to pay
Example: Before building HR automation: check what companies spend on recruiters (salary proxy) + ATS tools (SaaS proxy) + job board ads (ad spend proxy). If combined ~K/yr per company there is budget to displace.

Keywords: tam,sam,som,bottom up,sub market,niche,f1,f2,market sizing,market segmentation,total addressable market
Description: Avoid top-down TAM delusion. Drill down: TAM (total industry) → F1 sub-market (same characteristics segment 20-50% of TAM) → F2 niche (hyper-specific where you can be #1 immediately 5-15% of SAM). F2 is your real starting market. Validate F2 bottom-up: number of target customers × willingness to pay.
Framework: IdeaValidator TAM Funnel: TAM (total) → F1 (sub-market by geography/demo/behavior) → F2 (niche where you win day 1). Validate F2 via Google Trends + SimilarWeb + LinkedIn polls + Facebook Group surveys (50 responses minimum).
Do_This: Start with F2 not TAM — find the niche where you can be #1 today|Use bottom-up: count actual target customers × ARPU|Validate with free tools: IdeaProof.io (AI TAM analysis) pmtoolkit.ai (calculator) Google Trends (demand trend)|Cross-check with 50-person survey in target community
Avoid_This: Citing billion-dollar TAMs in pitch decks without F2 drill-down|Using only top-down estimates from industry reports|Targeting sub-market (F1) before proving niche (F2)
Example: HR Tech TAM B → F1: Recruiting software for startups → F2: AI screening tool for Senior engineers in SEA. F2 has ~3000 companies × /mo ARPU = M addressable.
